overview.what_it_is: This is a structured review lesson for the PTE Academic item types studied in Lessons 8–15. Instead of repeating activities randomly, learners recall the skills required by each item type, identify strengths and recurring difficulties, compare current performance with earlier self-assessments, exchange practical solutions, and choose targeted follow-up practice.

format_facts.label: Lesson purpose
format_facts.value: Review, diagnose, discuss, and plan improvement across speaking, writing, reading, and listening.

format_facts.label: Coverage
format_facts.value: Describe image, Re-order paragraphs, Listening: Fill in the blanks, Write from dictation, reading multiple-choice items, listening multiple-choice items, Re-tell lecture, Summarize spoken text, Highlight correct summary, and Write essay.

format_facts.label: Recommended study time
format_facts.value: 45–60 minutes for an individual review or a focused pair or group session.

format_facts.label: Main outputs
format_facts.value: A review table, a comparison of earlier and current performance, a problem-solution log, and a targeted practice plan.

format_facts.label: Reference review
format_facts.value: Review the general preparation guidance and relevant speaking, writing, reading, and listening strategy sections in the Official Guide.

scoring_factors.name: Skill identification
scoring_factors.what_it_measures: Whether the learner can accurately connect each item type with the listening, speaking, reading, writing, or enabling skills it requires.

scoring_factors.name: Problem diagnosis
scoring_factors.what_it_measures: Whether the learner can describe a specific performance problem instead of using a vague statement such as 'I am bad at listening.'

scoring_factors.name: Strategy relevance
scoring_factors.what_it_measures: Whether the selected solution directly addresses the identified problem and fits the item type.

scoring_factors.name: Progress evidence
scoring_factors.what_it_measures: Whether the learner can compare earlier and current responses using observable evidence such as fewer pauses, better recall, improved ordering, or fewer spelling errors.

scoring_factors.name: Action planning
scoring_factors.what_it_measures: Whether the learner chooses focused, repeatable practice with a clear goal rather than reviewing all item types equally.

critical_rules: Name the skill behind the item type before choosing another practice activity.
Describe problems specifically, including what happened, when it happened, and what effect it had on the response.
Use your own words during the first recall stage instead of immediately copying skill descriptions from a guide.
Compare current performance with an earlier response, recording, score, or assessment form whenever possible.
Choose extra practice according to your weakest high-impact skill, not according to which activity feels easiest.
Turn every identified problem into one practical strategy and one measurable follow-up action.

learning_goals: Recall the item types covered in Lessons 8–15 and explain the main skills required for each one.
Separate item-type knowledge from the underlying language skills being tested.
Identify confident areas and problem areas using specific evidence from previous practice.
Explain at least one recurring problem and match it with a practical improvement strategy.
Compare an earlier self-assessment with a current assessment and describe observable progress.
Use peer discussion to collect alternative solutions without copying strategies uncritically.
Choose targeted extra practice for speaking, writing, reading, and listening.
Create a realistic short-term plan for the next stage of PTE Academic preparation.

core_method.name: REPAIR Review Cycle
core_method.summary: Use a six-stage cycle to turn previous practice into an improvement plan: Recall the item type, Explain the skills, Pinpoint the problem, Ask for or generate solutions, Implement one targeted drill, and Review the result.

steps.detail: List the item types from Lessons 8–15 without consulting notes first. Add the basic task required for each item type.
State the main communicative and enabling skills needed, using your own words. For integrated tasks, name every skill involved.
Identify one precise difficulty from previous practice, such as losing the lecture sequence, misreading referents, pausing too often, or missing plural endings.
Discuss the difficulty with a partner or examine earlier strategy notes. Collect possible solutions, then reject any solution that does not directly address the problem.
Repeat one short activity while focusing on only the selected problem area. Avoid trying to correct every weakness in the same attempt.
Compare the new response with the earlier one, record what improved and what remains difficult, and decide the next action.

core_method.formula: Item type + required skill + specific problem + targeted strategy + evidence after practice = useful recap

techniques.name: Item-Type Skill Mapping
techniques.purpose: To connect each PTE task with the exact skills that produce a successful response.
how_to: Write the item type in the first column of a review log.
Describe what the test taker must do during the task.
List the communicative skills involved: speaking, writing, reading, or listening.
Add enabling skills such as fluency, pronunciation, grammar, spelling, vocabulary, or written discourse.
Check the Official Guide only after completing the first version in your own words.
techniques.example: Re-tell lecture: listen for the main idea and supporting points, take selective notes, preserve the lecture sequence, and speak fluently from those notes.
techniques.why_it_matters: A learner cannot choose effective practice until the true skill behind the difficulty is clear.
techniques.common_error: Writing only a broad label such as 'listening' without identifying note-taking, sequencing, recall, vocabulary, or inference.

techniques.name: Confidence–Evidence Check
techniques.purpose: To replace feelings about performance with observable evidence.
how_to: Give each skill a confidence rating from 1 to 5.
Write one piece of evidence supporting the rating.
Use a recording, corrected response, practice result, or repeated error as evidence.
Compare the rating with an earlier assessment.
Change the rating only when the evidence justifies it.
techniques.example: Describe image fluency: confidence 3 out of 5 because the response now continues for the full recording period, but there are still several long pauses before comparisons.
techniques.why_it_matters: Learners often overestimate familiar tasks and underestimate skills that have genuinely improved.
techniques.common_error: Giving a confidence score without explaining why the score was chosen.

techniques.name: Problem-to-Solution Conversion
techniques.purpose: To turn a weakness into a testable action rather than a general intention.
how_to: Describe the exact problem using one sentence.
Identify the stage where the problem occurs: preparation, comprehension, planning, response, or checking.
Choose one strategy that targets that stage.
Define a short drill that can be repeated immediately.
Decide what improvement would look like.
techniques.example: Problem: I forget the middle of a lecture. Stage: listening and note-taking. Strategy: divide notes into topic, point 1, point 2, and conclusion. Evidence: the next retell includes at least two supporting points in the correct order.
techniques.why_it_matters: Specific solutions are easier to practise, observe, and improve.
techniques.common_error: Using a solution such as 'practise more' without stating what to practise or how progress will be checked.

techniques.name: Second-Colour Progress Review
techniques.purpose: To make improvement and remaining weaknesses visible on an existing assessment form.
how_to: Find a self-assessment form completed earlier in the course.
Complete the same form again using a different colour or separate notation.
Circle areas with clear improvement.
Underline skills that remain difficult.
Write one next-step strategy beside every unchanged problem area.
techniques.example: Earlier: pronunciation was marked 'often unclear.' Current: 'usually clear, but word endings disappear when speaking quickly.' Next step: practise final consonants in short timed descriptions.
techniques.why_it_matters: The comparison shows progress that may be missed when learners focus only on current weaknesses.
techniques.common_error: Completing a new assessment but failing to compare it with the earlier version.

techniques.name: Single-Focus Repetition
techniques.purpose: To improve one weak skill without overloading attention.
how_to: Choose one previous practice item.
Select only one focus area before repeating it.
Complete the item under realistic conditions.
Review only the chosen feature during the first analysis.
Repeat the task once more using the correction.
techniques.example: Repeat a Re-order paragraphs task while checking only articles, pronoun referents, and discourse markers before considering the complete order.
techniques.why_it_matters: Trying to repair fluency, grammar, content, timing, and vocabulary at once makes improvement difficult to measure.
techniques.common_error: Changing several strategies in one attempt and then being unable to identify which change helped.

worked_examples.title: Three-Item Review Log
worked_examples.input: Create a review table for Describe image, Re-order paragraphs, and Re-tell lecture. Include the main skill, one problem, and one strategy.
worked_examples.decoding: The task requires three specific item types, an accurate skill connection, a real problem from practice, and a solution that directly targets that problem.
worked_examples.plan: For each row, write: task demand, underlying skill, observed difficulty, targeted drill, and expected evidence.
worked_examples.model_answer: Describe image — Main skills: visual analysis, organized speaking, fluency, and pronunciation. Problem: I spend too long listing small details and pause before the conclusion. Strategy: use a four-part plan: introduction, overview, two key features, conclusion, then practise with a 25-second speaking target. Re-order paragraphs — Main skills: identifying the topic sentence, referents, articles, discourse markers, and logical sequence. Problem: I connect sentences by topic only and ignore grammatical links. Strategy: mark every pronoun, article, and connector before arranging the full sequence. Re-tell lecture — Main skills: listening for the main idea, note-taking, recall, sequencing, and fluent delivery. Problem: my notes contain too many complete sentences, so I miss later points. Strategy: write keywords and symbols under topic, point 1, point 2, and conclusion.

annotations.comment: The problem identifies both content selection and fluency instead of saying only that speaking is difficult.
The strategy targets grammatical cohesion, which is the stated weakness.
The note format reduces writing load and protects listening attention.
Each solution can be tested immediately on one repeated item.

worked_examples.title: Progress Comparison
worked_examples.input: Compare an earlier speaking assessment with a current one and record one improvement, one remaining problem, and one next solution.
worked_examples.decoding: The response must show a time comparison, use evidence, and provide a next action for the unresolved difficulty.
worked_examples.plan: Select one speaking item, compare two recordings or assessment forms, and write three short statements.
worked_examples.model_answer: Improvement: My current Describe image response is more continuous because I use a fixed order and no longer restart sentences after small mistakes. Remaining problem: important words are sometimes unclear because I rush through numbers and final consonants. Next solution: I will practise short descriptions containing dates, percentages, and plural endings, record them, and check whether each key word is understandable.

annotations.comment: The learner gives evidence: fewer restarts and more continuous delivery.
The issue is narrowed to pronunciation during numbers and final consonants.
The drill repeats the exact language feature causing the problem.
Recording and checking intelligibility provide observable evidence.

worked_examples.title: Selecting Targeted Extra Practice
worked_examples.input: Choose one focus area from the lesson overview and explain why it fits the relevant item type.
worked_examples.decoding: A strong response must name the item type, select a relevant skill, explain the connection, and define a suitable practice activity.
worked_examples.plan: Use the pattern: item type, focus area, reason, drill, success indicator.
worked_examples.model_answer: For Summarize spoken text, I will focus on signpost vocabulary because words such as 'firstly,' 'however,' 'for example,' and 'in conclusion' reveal the structure of the recording. My drill will be to listen once and write only the signposts and the main point that follows each one. Success will mean that my final summary includes the central idea and the major supporting points in the correct relationship.

annotations.comment: Signpost vocabulary directly supports lecture organization and note-taking.
Writing only signposts and main points keeps the drill focused.
The learner checks both content coverage and logical relationship.
The same skill can also support Highlight correct summary and Re-tell lecture.

worked_examples.title: Group Problem-Solving Discussion
worked_examples.input: A learner says, 'I usually miss answers in Write from dictation because the sentence disappears from my memory.' Suggest a practical group solution.
worked_examples.decoding: The problem is not only spelling; it concerns listening, short-term recall, sequencing, and reconstruction.
worked_examples.plan: Clarify the failure point, suggest two possible strategies, select one immediate drill, and define what the group should observe.
worked_examples.model_answer: The group should first check whether the learner loses the whole sentence or only the middle section. A useful solution is chunked recall: listen for meaningful word groups, repeat the groups silently, write the content words first, and then reconstruct grammar words and endings. The group can practise with one sentence at a time and compare which chunks each person remembered. If the sentence order improves but spelling remains weak, spelling should become the next separate focus.

annotations.comment: The group investigates the exact location of the memory failure.
Meaningful groups reduce the burden on short-term memory.
Writing key words first protects the main sentence meaning.
Spelling is treated as a later focus instead of being mixed with recall practice.

items.item: I am more confident with ___ because ___.
items.when_to_use: Use this when giving evidence for an improved item type or skill.

items.item: Compared with my earlier response, I now ___.
items.when_to_use: Use this when comparing two recordings, written responses, or assessment forms.

items.item: This skill has improved, although I still need to work on ___.
items.when_to_use: Use this when progress is clear but incomplete.

items.item: The strongest evidence of progress is ___.
items.when_to_use: Use this to support a confidence judgment with an observable result.

items.item: The main difficulty occurs when ___.
items.when_to_use: Use this to identify the exact stage where performance breaks down.

items.item: I understand the task, but I lose accuracy when ___.
items.when_to_use: Use this to separate task knowledge from performance under pressure.

items.item: My response is affected by ___, which causes ___.
items.when_to_use: Use this to explain the connection between a weakness and its result.

items.item: This is mainly a problem with ___ rather than ___.
items.when_to_use: Use this to distinguish similar issues, such as recall versus spelling.

items.item: A practical way to improve this is to ___.
items.when_to_use: Use this when proposing a clear action.

items.item: The strategy fits the problem because ___.
items.when_to_use: Use this to justify why a solution is relevant.

items.item: For the next attempt, focus only on ___.
items.when_to_use: Use this when setting up single-focus repetition.

items.item: We can measure improvement by checking whether ___.
items.when_to_use: Use this to define observable success.

items.item: What exactly happened during the task?
items.when_to_use: Use this before offering advice so the problem is clearly understood.

items.item: Which part of the strategy helped you most?
items.when_to_use: Use this to identify a transferable technique from a partner.

items.item: Could the problem come from ___ instead?
items.when_to_use: Use this to consider an alternative diagnosis.

items.item: Let us check the guide to confirm that point.
items.when_to_use: Use this after group discussion when an item rule or strategy remains uncertain.

items.item: First, the item requires ___.
items.when_to_use: Use this to begin an explanation of task demands.

items.item: The main skill involved is ___, while a supporting skill is ___.
items.when_to_use: Use this to distinguish primary and secondary skills.

items.item: However, my current problem is ___.
items.when_to_use: Use this to move from task description to personal diagnosis.

items.item: Therefore, my next practice activity will be ___.
items.when_to_use: Use this to connect the diagnosis with an action plan.

common_mistakes.mistake: Treating the recap as a memory quiz about item-type names.
common_mistakes.why_it_hurts: Knowing a task name does not show that the learner understands the skills, problems, or strategies connected with it.
common_mistakes.fix: For every item type, add the task demand, skills required, one problem, and one next action.

common_mistakes.mistake: Reviewing every skill for the same amount of time.
common_mistakes.why_it_hurts: Limited study time is spent on already strong areas while important weaknesses remain untreated.
common_mistakes.fix: Prioritize high-impact problems and use targeted extra practice.

common_mistakes.why_it_hurts: Statements such as 'my listening is poor' do not reveal which drill would help.
common_mistakes.fix: Name the exact failure, such as missing contrast markers, losing sentence endings, or recording too many notes.

common_mistakes.mistake: Opening the Official Guide before trying to recall the skills independently.
common_mistakes.why_it_hurts: The learner may copy terminology without checking whether the skill is genuinely understood.
common_mistakes.fix: Complete an initial skill map in your own words, then verify and correct it using the guide.

common_mistakes.why_it_hurts: A popular strategy may not address the learner's actual problem or may add unnecessary complexity.
common_mistakes.fix: Ask how the suggestion targets the identified failure and test it on one short practice item.

common_mistakes.why_it_hurts: A score may change without showing which part of performance improved or declined.
common_mistakes.fix: Compare process evidence such as note quality, response structure, fluency, error type, timing, and content coverage.

common_mistakes.mistake: Trying to repair several weaknesses in one repetition.
common_mistakes.why_it_hurts: Attention becomes overloaded and the learner cannot tell which strategy caused improvement.
common_mistakes.fix: Use one focus per attempt, then select a different focus in the next cycle.

common_mistakes.mistake: Ending the recap without scheduling further practice.
common_mistakes.why_it_hurts: Discussion creates awareness but does not produce improvement unless it leads to action.
common_mistakes.fix: Finish with a specific item type, drill, frequency, and success indicator.

time_budget.focus: List the Lessons 8–15 item types and describe the main task for each without using reference materials.
Connect each item type to its communicative and enabling skills.
Rate confidence, add evidence, and identify one precise problem for selected item types.
Share difficulties, generate possible strategies, and choose the most relevant solution.
Repeat one or two previous activities using a single improvement focus.
Compare results, record improvement, and schedule the next focused practice.

drills.name: One-Minute Item Recall
drills.instructions: Choose an item type and explain in one minute: what the task requires, which skills it tests, one common problem, and one useful strategy.

drills.name: Skill Sorting
drills.instructions: Write the item types on separate cards or lines and classify them under speaking, writing, reading, listening, or integrated. Add enabling skills beside each one.

drills.name: Problem Ladder
drills.instructions: Start with a vague difficulty such as 'weak listening.' Ask 'What exactly goes wrong?' three times until the problem becomes specific enough for a targeted drill.

drills.name: Strategy Match
drills.instructions: Prepare several problem statements and several strategies. Match each problem to the most suitable strategy and explain why the other strategies are less relevant.

drills.name: Before-and-After Comparison
drills.instructions: Use two responses to the same item type. Record one improvement in task completion, one improvement in language, and one remaining weakness.

drills.name: Single-Focus Repeat
drills.instructions: Repeat one previous item while concentrating on only one area, such as pronunciation, referents, note-taking, signposts, spelling, or paragraph structure.

practice_plan.routine: At the end of each future practice session, spend five minutes completing four lines: item practised, strongest feature, exact problem, and next drill. At the end of the week, select the two most repeated problems and build the following week's study plan around them.

mastery_checklist: I can name the major item types reviewed in Lessons 8–15.
I can explain what each reviewed item type requires the test taker to do.
I can identify the communicative and enabling skills behind each item type.
I can distinguish a task-format problem from a language-skill problem.
I can describe at least three personal problem areas using specific evidence.
I can match each identified problem with a practical strategy.
I can compare an earlier and current response and state what improved.
I can explain what remains difficult without ignoring the progress already made.
I can use peer feedback critically rather than accepting every suggestion.
I can choose extra practice based on my actual problem areas.
I can define what successful improvement will look or sound like.
I have a realistic plan for continued speaking, writing, reading, and listening practice.
strategy_notes: Describe image review should prioritize selecting key features, organizing the response, maintaining fluency, and producing clear pronunciation rather than naming every visible detail.
Re-order paragraphs review should include topic sentences, articles, pronoun referents, repeated key terms, discourse markers, cause-and-effect links, and chronological sequence.

Listening: Fill in the blanks and Write from dictation should be reviewed separately when the main problem differs, because one may involve following a transcript while the other depends heavily on recall and reconstruction.
Reading multiple-choice review should distinguish gist, writer purpose, detail, inference, and option elimination; the prompt determines which reading strategy is needed.
Listening multiple-choice review should separate the main idea from supporting examples and redundant information before evaluating answer options.
Re-tell lecture practice should use selective notes, clear lecture structure, and fluent reconstruction instead of attempting to reproduce every sentence.
Summarize spoken text and Highlight correct summary benefit from recognizing signposts, speaker attitude, major supporting points, and irrelevant or contradictory information.
Write essay review should include prompt interpretation, planning, paragraph organization, supporting explanations, grammar, spelling, and final editing rather than focusing only on vocabulary.
When an unresolved question concerns an official task rule, verify it using the relevant Official Guide section instead of relying on group memory.
A recap is successful when it changes the next practice decision, not merely when the learner completes a review worksheet.
